headline: After the
shortage.
dek: The GLP-1 shortages are over. FDA says what pharmacies may still compound.
photoAlt: A line cook in a black work shirt holds a folded notice.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Oct 31, 2026 · Clinical review pending

pull.quote: Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. This means the agency does not review their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.

body: For more than two years, the most famous weight drugs in the country were in short supply, and pharmacies were allowed to fill the gap with their own versions. That window has closed. FDA said the shortage of [[/tirzepatide|tirzepatide]] injection was resolved on December 19, 2024, and the shortage of [[/semaglutide|semaglutide]] injection on February 21, 2025.[^apr] The grace periods for compounders ran out in the spring of 2025, and on April 1, 2026, FDA said neither drug is on its shortage list.[^apr]

What pharmacies may do now is narrower. They can still compound for an individual patient, but they may not regularly make drugs that are essentially copies of a product on the market. FDA’s April 2026 statement gave a worked example: a compounded injection that combines semaglutide with vitamin B12 can count as a copy when both amounts are within 10% of the strengths of available products, unless a prescriber documents a significant difference for that patient.[^apr] FDA added a limit on how hard it will push: it said it “does not intend to take action against a compounder for compounding a drug product that is essentially a copy of a commercially available drug product regularly or in inordinate amounts if the compounder fills four or fewer prescriptions of that compounded drug product during a calendar month.”[^apr] It gave no tirzepatide example.

Compounded versions are not FDA approved, whatever is added to them. In a March 2026 news release announcing 30 warning letters to telehealth companies, FDA put it plainly: “Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. This means the agency does not review their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.”[^pr] The letters, it said, mostly concerned “claims implying sameness with FDA-approved products.”[^pr] None of the large trials behind the brands tested semaglutide or tirzepatide mixed with vitamin B12 or glycine.

The approved brands are a different thing. Semaglutide is sold as Ozempic and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes and as Wegovy for weight and heart risk.[^ozempic][^wegovy] Tirzepatide is sold as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and as Zepbound for weight and obstructive sleep apnea.[^mounjaro][^zepbound] Using one of the diabetes brands for weight loss is off-label. In April 2026 a third option arrived: FDA approved [[/orforglipron|orforglipron]], a pill, as Foundayo for weight management in adults.[^foundayo]

An older drug in the same family is in a different position. [[/liraglutide|Liraglutide]] is approved as Victoza for type 2 diabetes and as Saxenda for weight management.[^victoza][^saxenda] Yet FDA’s shortage records still list liraglutide injection as in shortage, a listing that began in July 2023, and they show Saxenda as due to be discontinued.[^short] That keeps the question of compounded copies open for this one drug in a way it no longer is for semaglutide and tirzepatide.

The trials behind the brands were large, and they were paid for by the companies that make the drugs. In STEP 1, adults with obesity or overweight took weekly semaglutide or a placebo for 68 weeks; “the mean change in body weight from baseline to week 68 was -14.9% in the semaglutide group as compared with -2.4% with placebo.”[^step1] In SURMOUNT-1, adults without diabetes took one of three weekly doses of tirzepatide or a placebo for 72 weeks, and average weight fell by 15.0% to 20.9% on the drug and 3.1% on placebo.[^surmount]

These drugs come with FDA’s strongest warning. The Wegovy label opens with a boxed warning that “in rodents, semaglutide causes dose-dependent and treatment-duration-dependent thyroid C-cell tumors at clinically relevant exposures,”[^wegovy] and that it is unknown whether the drug causes them in people. People with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer, or with MEN 2 syndrome, must not use it.[^wegovy] The tirzepatide labels have the same kind of warning, and the Foundayo label does too.[^zepbound][^foundayo] The labels also list pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, kidney injury from dehydration, and severe stomach and bowel effects.[^wegovy]

FDA keeps count of problems with the compounded versions. It said that as of May 31, 2026, it had received 990 reports of adverse events tied to compounded semaglutide and more than 730 tied to compounded tirzepatide.[^con] It cautioned that “it is not always possible to determine if the adverse event directly resulted from use of the drug or if other factors may have contributed to these adverse events.”[^con] It has also received reports, some requiring hospital care, that may be related to dosing errors with compounded semaglutide, from patients measuring the wrong dose and, in some cases, health care professionals miscalculating it.[^con]

The next wave of weight drugs is already being sold before it is approved. [[/retatrutide|Retatrutide]] is in Phase 3 trials, and [[/cagrilintide|cagrilintide]] is being tested with semaglutide. FDA says retatrutide and cagrilintide “cannot be used in compounding under federal law.”[^con] It also says it has warned companies that illegally sold unapproved drugs containing semaglutide, tirzepatide, retatrutide, [[/survodutide|survodutide]] or [[/mazdutide|mazdutide]] “that are falsely labeled”[^con] as for research purposes or not for human consumption. FDA says these products were sold directly to consumers with dosing instructions, and urges people not to buy them.[^con]

Older drugs have not gone away. [[/phentermine|Phentermine]], an appetite suppressant, is approved for short-term use and is a Schedule IV controlled substance.[^lomaira] FDA approved it with [[/topiramate|topiramate]] as Qsymia, for long-term weight management, in 2012.[^qsymiaapp][^qsymia] [[/naltrexone|Naltrexone]] and [[/bupropion|bupropion]] are approved together as Contrave,[^contrave] and [[/orlistat|orlistat]] is sold by prescription as Xenical and over the counter as Alli.[^xenical][^alli]

What is still unknown is how compounded copies compare with the brands they imitate, since no trial has tested them, and how often their adverse events happen, since most pharmacies do not have to report them. For now, the approved brands have the trials, the boxed warnings and FDA’s review. The copies have none of those.
